title: React Router: Navigation and URL Params

subChunks.title: React Router: Navigation and URL Params
subChunks.hookHtml: Single-page apps don't reload the page when navigating — they swap components. React Router gives your app URL-based navigation: different URLs render different components, the back button works, and links are shareable. It's the difference between an app and a demo.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Setup

// main.jsx
import { BrowserRouter } from 'react-router-dom';

createRoot(document.getElementById('root')).render(
  <BrowserRouter>
    <App />
  </BrowserRouter>
);

Defining routes

import { Routes, Route } from 'react-router-dom';

function App() {
  return (
    <Routes>
      <Route path="/" element={<HomePage />} />
      <Route path="/quests" element={<QuestListPage />} />
      <Route path="/quests/:id" element={<QuestDetailPage />} />
      <Route path="*" element={<NotFoundPage />} />
    </Routes>
  );
}

Navigation — Link and useNavigate

import { Link, useNavigate } from 'react-router-dom';

// Declarative:
<Link to="/quests">View Quests</Link>

// Programmatic (after an action):
const navigate = useNavigate();
navigate('/quests'); // call inside handlers

Always use <Link> instead of <a href> for internal navigation. <a> triggers a full page reload.

Reading URL parameters

import { useParams } from 'react-router-dom';

// Route: /quests/:id
function QuestDetailPage() {
  const { id } = useParams(); // always a string
  const questId = parseInt(id, 10);
}

Nested routes and shared layouts

function App() {
  return (
    <Routes>
      <Route path="/" element={<Layout />}>
        <Route index element={<HomePage />} />
        <Route path="quests" element={<QuestListPage />} />
        <Route path="quests/:id" element={<QuestDetailPage />} />
      </Route>
    </Routes>
  );
}

import { Outlet } from 'react-router-dom';
function Layout() {
  return (
    <>
      <nav><Link to="/">Home</Link> | <Link to="/quests">Quests</Link></nav>
      <main><Outlet /></main>
    </>
  );
}

Vex: "The Outlet component is where React Router renders the matched child route inside a layout. Without an Outlet, nested child routes never appear."

storyBeats.speaker: Vex the Interface Weaver
storyBeats.text: A real app has multiple pages. React Router gives URLs meaning without reloading the page. Different URLs render different components. The back button works. Links can be bookmarked and shared. Without routing, you have a demo. With routing, you have an app.

storyBeats.speaker: Routes, Link, and useParams

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Build a two-page app with React Router:

  • Home page (/): renders <h1 data-testid="home">Home</h1> and a <Link to="/about">About</Link>
  • About page (/about): renders <h1 data-testid="about">About</h1> and a <Link to="/">Home</Link>
  • A catch-all * route that renders <p data-testid="404">Page not found</p>
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Build a mini quest browser from scratch with three pages: a list page at / that shows three quests as Links to /quests/:id; a detail page at /quests/:id that shows the quest ID; and a 404 page. Use a shared Layout with a persistent nav bar. No scaffold.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain the difference between `<a href>` and `<Link>` for internal navigation. What does each do to the browser? When would you use `useNavigate` instead of `<Link>`?

questions.prompt: What is the difference between `<a href="/about">` and `<Link to="/about">` in a React Router app?
options: <a> causes a full page reload; <Link> uses client-side navigation without reloading
They are functionally identical — React Router intercepts all <a> tags
<Link> is slower because it re-renders the entire app on navigation
<a> is required for accessibility; <Link> should only be used for buttons
questions.answer: <a> causes a full page reload; <Link> uses client-side navigation without reloading
questions.explanation: A standard <a href> makes the browser request a new URL and reload the entire page — losing React state. React Router's <Link> pushes to the browser's history API without a page reload. Always use <Link> for internal navigation.

questions.prompt: The route `/quests/:id` is matched. How do you access the `id` value inside the component?
questions.explanation: useParams() returns an object containing all dynamic segments from the matched URL. Note that URL params are always strings — parse to a number if needed.

questions.prompt: After a form submission succeeds, you want to redirect the user to `/dashboard`. Which React Router tool do you use?
options: useNavigate — call navigate('/dashboard') in the submit handler after the async action succeeds
Link — render <Link to="/dashboard" /> in the form's onSubmit
useLocation — update the current location object
Route — add a redirect Route that activates on form success
questions.answer: useNavigate — call navigate('/dashboard') in the submit handler after the async action succeeds
questions.explanation: Link is for declarative navigation via clicking. useNavigate is for programmatic navigation triggered by code — after a successful API call, after a timeout, or after any non-click event.

questions.prompt: You have a Layout component with a nav bar that should appear on every page. Which React Router feature renders the matched child route inside Layout?
options: <Outlet /> — a placeholder component from react-router-dom that renders the current child route
props.children — pass the current page as children to Layout
<Route /> — nest a Route inside Layout's JSX
useLocation() — read the current path and conditionally render the right component
questions.answer: <Outlet /> — a placeholder component from react-router-dom that renders the current child route
questions.explanation: When you use nested routes (<Route element={<Layout />}> with child <Route> elements inside), React Router renders Layout's element and replaces <Outlet /> with the matched child route's element.
